question: What is the primary definition of dysmenorrhoea?

options.A: Painful menstrual periods that interfere with daily activities
options.B: Infection of the uterine lining during the postpartum period
options.C: Abnormally heavy bleeding during the regular menstrual cycle
options.D: The complete absence of menstrual bleeding for over six months

explanation: Dysmenorrhoea specifically refers to painful menstruation that is severe enough to disrupt a person's normal daily routine. [learn more](GNS216_U2_T6#GNS216_U2_T6_h1)

question: Why must nurses always take complaints of menstrual pain seriously?

options.A: It is a legal requirement to report menstrual cramps to public health boards
options.B: Severe pain always indicates an underlying malignant tumour in the uterus
options.C: Menstrual pain is often dismissed despite being disabling for the patient
options.D: Pain during menstruation is extremely rare and requires immediate surgery

explanation: You got it! People often brush off menstrual cramps as 'normal,' so as nurses, our validation and compassionate care make a real difference.

question: Which chemical substance is primarily responsible for causing uterine contractions and pain in dysmenorrhoea?
explanation: Prostaglandins build up in the uterine lining and stimulate strong contractions of the uterine muscle, leading to cramping pain. [learn more](GNS216_U2_T6#GNS216_U2_T6_h2)

question: Why do some women experience upset stomach or diarrhoea along with their menstrual cramps?

options.A: The uterus physically presses directly against the stomach and bowels
options.B: Infection spreads rapidly from the pelvis to the gastrointestinal tract
options.C: Prostaglandins enter the bloodstream and affect other body systems
options.D: Hormonal shifts cause a sudden increase in daily food poisoning rates

explanation: Exactly! Prostaglandins don't just stay in the uterus; when they travel through the bloodstream, they can also stimulate the digestive tract.

question: What is the main difference between primary and secondary dysmenorrhoea?

options.A: Secondary dysmenorrhoea never involves cramping in the lower abdomen
options.B: Primary dysmenorrhoea is caused by abnormal growths in the uterus
options.C: Primary dysmenorrhoea only affects women over forty years of age
options.D: Secondary dysmenorrhoea is caused by an underlying pelvic pathology

explanation: Primary dysmenorrhoea has no structural cause, whereas secondary dysmenorrhoea stems from a specific disease process like fibroids or endometriosis. [learn more](GNS216_U2_T6#GNS216_U2_T6_h3)

question: A 32-year-old woman who has always had painless periods suddenly develops severe, worsening cramps during every cycle over the last year. Which condition is she most likely experiencing?
explanation: Onset of severe menstrual pain later in life, especially when it progressively worsens, is a classic sign of secondary dysmenorrhoea. [learn more](GNS216_U2_T6#GNS216_U2_T6_h3)

question: Which of these is a known risk factor for developing severe menstrual cramps?

options.A: Living in a warm tropical climate
options.B: Starting menstrual periods at a very early age
options.C: Having a short duration of menstrual bleeding
options.D: Starting menstruation after age sixteen years

explanation: Correct! Early menarche (getting your period before age 11) is linked to a higher chance of primary dysmenorrhoea.

question: Why does having a family history of menstrual pain increase a young person's chance of having dysmenorrhoea?

options.A: Genetic factors influence prostaglandin production and pain sensitivity
options.B: Pain is a learned behavior that is copied from older relatives
options.C: Mothers intentionally pass uterine infections down to their daughters
options.D: Family members usually share identical dietary habits every day

explanation: You got it! Genetics play a big role in how our bodies handle inflammatory chemicals and how sensitive we are to pain.

question: When do primary menstrual cramps usually hurt the most?

options.A: Exactly halfway through the normal menstrual cycle
options.B: During the first twenty-four hours of menstruation
options.C: On the final day when bleeding has nearly stopped
options.D: Two weeks before the menstrual bleeding begins

explanation: Spot on! Prostaglandin levels peak right at the start of your period, which is why the first day is usually the most painful.

question: Why is it helpful for a nurse to check how much menstrual pain affects a patient's daily routine?

options.A: To determine how severely the pain interferes with the patient's life
options.B: To decide whether the patient needs immediate emergency surgery
options.C: To prove to the physician that the patient is exaggerating symptoms
options.D: To calculate the exact financial cost of missed work days

explanation: Brilliant! Understanding how much pain disrupts their day helps us gauge the severity and plan the best care.

question: Which test is most commonly used to check for structural causes of secondary dysmenorrhoea?
explanation: Correct! An ultrasound is safe, non-invasive, and great for taking a look at the uterus and ovaries.

question: When should a nurse recommend a deeper medical checkup beyond basic history-taking for menstrual pain?

options.A: When the patient is a teenager experiencing her very first periods
options.B: When mild cramping is relieved easily by simple rest and warmth
options.C: When there is a strong family history of normal menstruation
options.D: When secondary dysmenorrhoea or pelvic pathology is suspected

explanation: You nailed it! If standard relief doesn't work or pain starts later in life, we need to investigate deeper for conditions like endometriosis.

question: Which type of medication is usually given first for primary dysmenorrhoea?
explanation: Spot on! NSAIDs like ibuprofen tackle the root cause by directly blocking prostaglandin production.

question: A patient asks when is the best time to take her ibuprofen for menstrual cramps. What should the nurse say?

options.A: Take it every morning for the entire month regardless of symptoms
options.B: Take the medication only after your menstrual bleeding stops
options.C: Wait until the pain becomes unbearable before taking any pill
options.D: Take it at the very start of your period or when pain begins

explanation: Well done! NSAIDs work best when taken early, before prostaglandins have a chance to build up and cause severe pain.

question: What is a major goal of teaching a patient who experiences dysmenorrhoea?

options.A: To convince the patient to avoid all physical movement during menstruation
options.B: To ensure the patient stops taking all prescribed medications immediately
options.C: To empower the patient with self-care techniques and pain management strategies
options.D: To discourage the patient from discussing menstrual health with relatives

explanation: Correct! Good education gives patients practical tools like heat therapy and proper medication use so they feel in control.

question: Which symptom should a nurse teach a patient with dysmenorrhoea to report immediately?

options.A: Feeling tired and needing extra sleep during bleeding
options.B: Mild lower abdominal cramping on the first day of menses
options.C: Sudden high fever and foul-smelling vaginal discharge
options.D: A slight decrease in appetite during the menstrual cycle

explanation: You got it! Fever and foul discharge are red flags for an infection, which means it's not just regular period pain and needs urgent attention.
